⚠️ Alleged Habib Metropolitan Bank Data Leak Exposes Customer PII on Darkweb  A post on an underground forum claims to have obtained sensitive customer data from Habib Metropolitan Bank Limited (HMB), a major commercial bank in Pakistan. The listing, titled "HABIB METROPOLITAN BANK LTD DATA," displays sample records containing personally identifiable information (PII) and financial account details for numerous individuals.  The leaked dataset appears to include the following fields: *   Full names of account holders *   National Identity Card (CNIC) numbers *   Residential addresses *   Bank branch codes and names *   Account numbers and types *   Currency and balance information  Habib Metropolitan Bank is one of Pakistan's largest private-sector banks, serving millions of customers across the country. The exposure of CNIC numbers alongside bank account details poses a significant risk to affected individuals, potentially enabling identity theft, social engineering attacks, or targeted fraud. The data samples provided in the thread reference branches in Karachi, Lahore, and Sukkur, indicating a broad geographic scope within Pakistan.  At the time of reporting, the alleged breach has not been independently verified by Habib Metropolitan Bank or Pakistani cybersecurity authorities. The threat actor behind the post has not been identified in the source material, and no ransom demand was explicitly stated in the visible portion of the thread, though a Telegram contact was provided for further inquiries.  #DataBreach #HabibMetropolitanBank #PakistanCyber #PIIExposure #DarkWeb #ThreatIntelligence

🚨 Alleged Leak of 12.1 Million Hong Kong Citizen Records Posted on Darkweb  A darkweb forum post claims the release of a massive dataset containing personal information for 12.1 million individuals in Hong Kong. The listing, published on an underground marketplace, alleges that the data was compiled from various sources and includes sensitive personally identifiable information (PII) for a significant portion of the territory's population.  According to the thread, the dataset includes the following fields for each record:  - Name - ID Number - Gender - Birthday - Address - Zip Code - District Details (District 2, 3, and 4) - Mobile Phone Number - Landline Telephone Number - Email Address  The poster provided a link to a sample file hosted on a pastebin service to verify the authenticity of the data. If authentic, the exposure of such granular demographic and contact data could facilitate large-scale phishing campaigns, identity fraud, and targeted social engineering attacks against residents in the region.  Hong Kong has previously experienced significant data breaches, including incidents involving major telecommunications providers and government-related databases, highlighting persistent vulnerabilities in the region's data protection infrastructure. The scale of this alleged leak, covering over 12 million records, would represent one of the largest PII exposures in the area if verified.  At the time of reporting, the alleged breach has not been independently verified by authorities or security researchers.  #DataLeak #HongKong #PII #DarkWeb #IdentityTheft #CyberSecurity #ThreatIntelligence

🚨Threat Actor Claims Critical 0-Day in NZ Government Certificate API  A threat actor is offering a purported critical zero-day vulnerability for sale on an underground forum, alleging that the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs (DIA) has exposed its production certificate issuance API to unauthenticated attacks. The post claims the flaw allows attackers to create and modify citizen certificate orders without any form of authentication, potentially compromising the integrity of government records.  According to the listing, the vulnerability affects the DIA's REST API hosted on an Azure API Management gateway. The actor alleges that the endpoint enforces zero authentication, relying solely on a client-version header (X-Version) that can be easily extracted from public JavaScript bundles. The claimed impact includes the ability to submit fake orders with arbitrary Personally Identifiable Information (PII) such as names, dates of birth, and birthplaces into the production database.  The seller asserts that the flaw enables several critical actions, including: - Creating fake, persisted certificate orders with arbitrary citizen PII - Modifying existing orders via an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) write without ownership checks - Poisoning data integrity to cause operational disruption or identity fraud - Leaking internal backend infrastructure details via error responses  The Department of Internal Affairs is the primary government agency responsible for maintaining New Zealand's civil records, including births, deaths, marriages, and citizenship. A compromise of this system could have significant implications for national security and public trust in government digital services. The actor has listed the price for the full unredacted Proof of Concept (PoC) at $1,500, demanding payment before revealing the specific URLs, tenant details, and backend hosts.  At the time of reporting, the alleged breach has not been independently verified by the New Zealand government or security researchers. The DIA has not yet issued a public statement regarding the claim.  #NewZealand #DIA #ZeroDay #IDOR #AzureAPIM #DarkWeb #CyberSecurity

⚠️ UPDATE: PRE-PATCH STOPGAP FOR TWO CRITICAL PHP RCE FLAWS (CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619)  PHP's emergency release for two vulnerabilities, both rated CVSS v4.0 9.2, is scheduled for today, Oct 21 at 14:00 UTC (10:00 a.m. ET). PHP has published NO technical details, affected versions or fixed versions yet, and reserves the right to ship earlier if details leak or exploitation appears.  What's confirmed: • Two critical flaws, both CVSS v4.0 9.2, patches due Oct 21 14:00 UTC • php.net has withheld all technical detail until release; mainstream reporting notes the CVEs are real and may reach back to PHP 5  Unconfirmed researcher assessment (their own read of php-src, moderate confidence): • Likely path is session.upload_progress / multipart rfc1867 handling (php_session_rfc1867_callback) — present since PHP 5.4, on by default, reachable before authentication • A quoted post claims two heap use-after-free bugs there were recreated in a lab. Treat the root cause and the recreation claim as unverified until PHP's advisory confirms them.  ⚠️ Analyst Note (stopgap you can apply now, low-risk and reversible): • Set session.upload_progress.enabled = Off in php.ini / .user.ini, then reload PHP-FPM or your web server. By the researchers' own read this may close only one of the two likely paths. • Tighten WAF or reverse-proxy inspection of, or rate-limit, multipart/form-data POSTs to endpoints that don't need uploads — the second likely path runs for any multipart POST regardless of the setting. • Inventory every PHP host now and patch the moment the release lands. PHP 7.x and older are end-of-life and will NOT get a fix — plan to upgrade. No proof-of-concept or exploit detail is being shared. No active attacks have been established.  Credit to researchers @J4ck3LSyN, @acd421 and @ArchKnight23 for the early mitigation guidance.  Primary: jackalsyn[.]com · php.net · arstechnica[.]com  #PHP #CVE #RCE #CyberSecurity #ThreatIntelligence #PatchNow #DDW #DarkWeb

⚠️ UPDATE: PUBLIC EXPLOIT RELEASED FOR CRITICAL FORTISIEM UNAUTHENTICATED RCE (CVE-2026-106173)  Horizon3.ai published a technical deep-dive and proof-of-concept exploit on Oct 20, 2026 for CVE-2026-106173, the FortiSIEM flaw Fortinet patched on Oct 13.  • The phQueryMaster gRPC service listens on TCP 27918 on all interfaces and does not require a client certificate, so any remote client can reach it without authentication • A path traversal in the SendQueryResult handler gives an arbitrary file write, which Horizon3.ai chains into remote code execution • Fortinet's updated CVE record now lists FortiSIEM 7.0.0–7.0.4, 7.1.0–7.1.9, 7.2.0–7.2.7, 7.3.0–7.3.5, 7.4.0–7.4.2 and 7.5.0 as affected, not only 7.5.0 • Fix: upgrade to FortiSIEM 7.5.1+ or 7.6.0+ (CVSS 9.4)  ⚠️ Analyst Note: This is a public exploit, not confirmed attacks in the wild. CISA's Oct 20 enrichment of the CVE record marks proof-of-concept exploitation as available and automatable; the CVE was not in the KEV catalog when checked. With working exploit code now public, treat any FortiSIEM with TCP 27918 reachable from untrusted networks as urgent. Our Oct 14 post listed only 7.5.0 as affected; Fortinet has since widened the range. When we covered Plex2Shell on Oct 18, the Plex CVEs were not in KEV. Now they are.  What's new: • Plex Media Server: CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655 and CVE-2026-96656, the four flaws chained in Plex2Shell (SSRF, plugin call injection, arbitrary file write that runs on load) • Plex's own Oct 19 security update now confirms widespread exploitation: attackers are using the chain to install cryptocurrency miners and proxy software on internet-facing servers • SiteGuard Server Edition: CVE-2026-106931 OS command injection that can run commands as root or SYSTEM; the vendor confirmed abuse on Oct 14 • Siemens Software Center: CVE-2026-110936 DLL sideloading (CWE-427); Siemens SSA-580366 refers to known active exploitation • Federal due dates are Oct 23 (SiteGuard, two Plex CVEs) and Nov 3 (two Plex CVEs, Siemens); SiteGuard and CVE-2026-96656 are flagged for forensic triage • Ransomware use is listed as unknown for all six  Fixed: Plex Media Server 1.43.3.10861 or later. SiteGuard Server Edition Ver8.00 Update 5 (Ver7.00 Update 6 on FreeBSD) or the vendor patch. Siemens Software Center V4.0.9.8 (auto-updates on next startup).  ⚠️ Analyst Note: Plex servers exposed on port 32400 with a public PoC should be treated as possibly compromised if they ran older builds. Plex advises rebuilding from a clean installation when compromise cannot be ruled out; updating alone is not enough. For SiteGuard, save the Diagnostic information first, because patching can erase attack traces. They received an e-mail from a student (who has surely had their e-mail compromised) telling them they need to review the Universities conduct policy, or something, and they must install "Zoho Assist"   Zoho Assist is a legitimate tool for remotely assisting people. But, some dorky ass Threat Actor is sending out these goofy social engineering e-mails hoping a student will install Zoho on their devices  My question for the Threat Actor: what if the student isn't running Windows? There has been a glitch in the matrix. @smica83 shared a heavily obfuscated .vbs which was first identified in Morocco, initially named "nouveau_cv_pdf.vbs".  I wasn't going to statically deobfuscate the piece of shit, so I emulated it. During emulation it catches it pulling a stage 2 binary from: https://qmlab1(.)com/assets/img/katyusha2  I curl the payload, look inside, and you're never going to believe it.  It's the exact same fucking binary I just discussed. It is the Go malware labeled internally as "EasyAgent"  I've never accidentally stumbled upon the same malware campaign, with different delivery methods, back to back like this. This is very silly

> be me > get dm > "smelly, i found goop" > wtf i love goop (malware) > "Someone in South Korea received a Fortinet installer, except the "ipfilter" binary looks suspicious" > ok > download > look inside > goop malware left pdb intact > "E:\dropper_cpp\dropper\dropper" > ... > image 1 > lolwtf bro > downloads "install.exe" > http://52.74.54.75/storage/install.exe > install.exe is malware written Go > registers itself as a service > "EasyAgent" > unobfuscated > everything visible > "Easyagent_connection_Connect" > shows connecting to wss://52.74.54.75 > Image 2  dawg, if you're going to try to masquerade as a fortinet client thingie, and target large companies for initial access, you really need to up your goop game. this took me literally like, 2 minutes to reverse engineer and identify what you're doing.
